grammar_notes.title: Celebrating Milestones with 'Makorokoto!'
grammar_notes.content: The exclamation 'Makorokoto!' means 'Congratulations!'. To specify what you are congratulating someone for, attach the prefix 'ne-' ('for / with') directly to an infinitive verb starting with 'ku-'. In this sentence, 'nekubudirira' combines 'ne-' (for) + 'kubudirira' (to succeed), literally meaning 'for succeeding'.
grammar_notes.rule: Makorokoto + ne- + ku-[verb] = Congratulations on [doing something]! (e.g., Makorokoto nekubudirira!)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('kwenyu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'kwenyu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nekubudirira'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nekubudirira'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'kubudirira' forms 'nekubudirira'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

cultural_notes.title: Celebrating Shared Success ('Makorokoto!')
cultural_notes.content: Whenever someone passes an exam, starts a new job, welcomes a child, or achieves a goal, friends, neighbours, and family gather to say 'Makorokoto!' ('Congratulations!'). Success in Shona culture is celebrated as a shared achievement for the whole family and community, often accompanied by handshakes, ululation ('kupururudza'), and words of encouragement.

active_exercises.prompt: If a friend asks you in the afternoon 'Waswera sei?', what is the natural reply?
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, you reply to 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?') with 'Ndaswera kana waswerawo' ('I spent the day well if you spent it well too').

active_exercises.prompt: What is the difference between 'Mhoro' and 'Mhoroi'?
options: 'Mhoro' is used only at night, while 'Mhoroi' is used in the morning
'Mhoro' is for one peer/child, while 'Mhoroi' is for an elder or a group of people
'Mhoro' is used in shops, while 'Mhoroi' is used only at school
active_exercises.correct_answer: 'Mhoro' is for one peer/child, while 'Mhoroi' is for an elder or a group of people
active_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' ('Mhoro' -> 'Mhoroi') shows plural or respectful address.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you form ordinal numbers like 'first', 'second', and 'third' in Shona?
options: Place the word 'nhamba' after the verb
Attach '-ekutanga' (first), '-echipiri' (second), and '-echitatu' (third) with the noun's possessive prefix
active_exercises.correct_answer: Attach '-ekutanga' (first), '-echipiri' (second), and '-echitatu' (third) with the noun's possessive prefix
active_exercises.explanation: Ordinal numbers use '-ekutanga' (1st), '-echipiri' (2nd), '-echitatu' (3rd), e.g., 'zuva rechitatu' ('the third day').
